title: Ganges treaty panel signs off 2026 report in Dhaka; no date yet for renewal talks, 19 days before expiry
dek: The joint committee that monitors the Farakka water-sharing treaty finalised its annual report on Sunday. Bangladesh again urged India to open formal negotiations before the 1996 treaty expires on 12 December.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Indian and Bangladeshi officials finalised the annual report on how the Ganges water-sharing treaty was implemented in 2026 at a meeting in Dhaka on Sunday, but no date has been set for talks on what replaces the treaty when it expires on 12 December, now 19 days away. Bangladesh used the occasion to urge India again to take "necessary steps" to begin formal negotiations, according to reports from Dhaka.

Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, an adviser to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman who heads Bangladesh's technical committee on the treaty, said Bangladesh had finished its preparations and hoped India would act before the term runs out, according to reports. Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee has written to his Indian counterpart through diplomatic channels seeking an early start, and wants a new or revised agreement rather than a simple renewal. India's Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday that the Joint Rivers Commission is the established mechanism for water issues, including the Ganges, and that India remains committed to a constructive relationship while safeguarding its interests, according to reports. India has not announced a date for negotiations or for any interim arrangement.

## The Dhaka meeting

The 91st meeting of the India-Bangladesh Joint Committee, the body that oversees the treaty's joint monitoring teams at Farakka and at Hardinge Bridge in Bangladesh, was held in Dhaka on Sunday. The Indian team was led by Sharad Chandra, a commissioner in the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation and India's member on the Joint Rivers Commission, and included Sanjay Kumar Gangwar of the Central Water Commission. The six-member Bangladeshi delegation was led by Md Anwar Kadir, a member of the Joint Rivers Commission, according to reports.

The two sides finalised the 2026 annual implementation report, reports said. The committee has met alternately in the two countries since 1997, usually three times a year: in Kolkata after a field visit to Farakka, in Dhaka after a visit to Hardinge Bridge, and once to prepare the annual report. Its 89th meeting was in Dhaka on 8 April and its 90th in Kolkata on 22 May. Indian officials had described this meeting as routine, and reports from Dhaka did not say whether the treaty's future was discussed.

Bangladesh's ministers kept up the public push over the weekend. Bangladesh's foreign minister, speaking at the Indian Ocean Conference in Mauritius, said Dhaka wanted a durable new or revised arrangement that could anchor relations for the next 25 to 50 years, according to reports. Humaiun Kobir, the state minister for foreign affairs, said Bangladesh would seek an outcome that protects its interests, possibly including a guarantee clause.

## What Dhaka says

Mr Titumir has said the region that depends on the Ganges, known as the Padma in Bangladesh, covers about a third of the country and is home to more than five crore people.

Dhaka first told New Delhi in June that it had set up a high-level technical committee and asked India to name its own team, and repeated the request in August, according to reports. Mr Anee's priority is to restore a "guarantee clause" securing Bangladesh's share in the leanest weeks. A 1977 agreement between the two countries had such a safeguard: if the flow at Farakka fell short in any ten-day period, Bangladesh's release would not drop below 80% of its scheduled share, according to reports.

Humayun Kabir, a former Bangladeshi ambassador (not the state minister), said a meeting between the two prime ministers could settle on one of several options: renewing the treaty for another full term, a short extension, or a one- or two-year extension while it is reviewed. "We have to have some kind of agreement as soon as possible before this one expires," he said, according to reports.

## India's position

The Ministry of External Affairs has said all river matters, "including Ganga", are handled through the Joint Rivers Commission, the body the two countries set up in 1972. At its briefing on 3 November, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said there was no update on a meeting of the commission, and that India had invited Mr Rahman to visit. No visit has been announced. Bangladesh and India share 54 rivers; the Ganges is the only one covered by a water-sharing treaty.

India has been consulting its own states. West Bengal attended four meetings of an inter-ministerial review committee between October 2023 and March 2025, and Bihar attended four between August 2023 and May 2024, according to reports. West Bengal has asked for adequate dry-season flows down the Bhagirathi-Hooghly, which carries water to Kolkata and its port. In July, Parliament's Standing Committee on External Affairs urged the government to finish its review and start talks with Bangladesh without further delay.

## What is at stake for Bengal

The treaty, signed on 12 December 1996, sets a formula for sharing the water that reaches Farakka from 1 January to 31 May each year. In the driest weeks, between 11 March and 10 May, each country is guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternating ten-day periods. A joint committee measures the flow every day at Farakka and at Hardinge Bridge in Bangladesh. Article XII says it can be renewed only "on the basis of mutual consent"; there is no automatic extension.

If no arrangement is in place by 12 December, the dry season of 2027, which begins less than three weeks later, would be the first since 1996 without an agreed sharing rule or joint measurement of the river. For West Bengal, the treaty decides how much water India can send down the feeder canal into the Hooghly in those months; for Bangladesh it governs the flow into the Padma and the south-west of the country.

## What happens next

The treaty runs until the end of 12 December. Any extension, interim arrangement or new treaty needs both governments to agree, and officials in Dhaka have said the decision will have to be taken at the political level. Neither side has announced a meeting of the Joint Rivers Commission or a summit between the prime ministers before then. The dry season covered by the treaty begins on 1 January.
